newsitem.title: USA: Details of balanced budget agreement.
newsitem.headline: Details of balanced budget agreement.

text.p: The White House and Republican and Democratic lawmakers reached agreeement on Friday on a plan to balance the budget by 2002 and provide tax cuts for millions of Americans.

The plan includes an overall tax cut of $135 billion spread over five years. This tax cut would be partially paid for with $50 billion in other taxes. While not specified in the budget, congressional sources said it was assumed the airline ticket tax would raise $35 billion and that user fees and other higher taxes would make up the remainder.

This net tax cut of $85 billion would include a $500 per child tax credit, a broad-based capital gains tax cut, relief from estate taxes paid on inheritances worth more than $600,000, and a tax break to help pay for higher education worth $35 billion over five years.
The specific tax rates would be set later by tax writing committees.

A major part of the savings required to bring down the deficit would be found in the Medicare health care programme for the elderly which would see a $115 billion reduction over five years. The plan is designed to keep the Medicare trust fund solvent until at least 2007.
The bulk of the Medicare savings would come from scaling back payments to doctors, hospitals, managed care plans and other health providers.

The final budget deal would slightly increase premiums under the optional Medicare Part B programme that covers doctors' care. Medicare recipients now pay $43.80 per month, 25 percent of the Part B premium.

It phases in a $1 per year increase in the premium over seven to 10 years to cover home health-care services that will be shifted from the Medicare hospital trust fund into Part B. The poor would be given an exemption.

The plan includes gross cuts of about $16 billion over five years in the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled. At the last minute, negotiators backed off a plan to set a per-person federal spending cap on the programme, which is now an open-ended entitlement, jointly funded by the states and Washington. The proposal includes cuts in Medicaid payments to hospitals that serve many poor people.

President Bill Clinton won $34 billion over five years for his initiatives including $16 billion to $17 billion for health insurance for 5 million children. The budget accord also restores medical disability benefits to legal immigrants who are now on the rolls. Some immigrants currently in the country may become eligible for the aid. Under the welfare law enacted last year, hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants will lose disability benefits this summer.

For other annually approved spending, the White House said funding will be within 1 percent of the president's request. This amount was adequate for education, the environment, foreign affairs and other programmes. For defence, the White House said Congress met their request for budget authority.
For education, the maximum Pell college grant would be raised to $3,000 and Clinton's "America Reads" programme was fully funded.
The administration's request for funds for cleanup of toxic waste sites was met, the White House said.
